ROCHE (Marquette) asked ;
1.	Has a petition been received by the_ government from the Indians of St. Peter's reserve, Manitoba, in reference to the holding of an election for chief and councillors?
2.	Is it necessary to receive the consent of the government before such an election can take place?
3.	What is the term of office they are elected for, and when does the term of the present chief and councillors expire?
4.	Will the surrender of the St. Peter's reserve interfere with the holding of their election ?	,
5.	What reply, if any, has been made by the government to the petition?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
1.	Yes ; a petition, dated 7th of January, 1908, has been received from the Indians of the St. Peter's reserve in reference to the holding of an election for chief and councillors.
2.	It is considered necessary that the consent of the government should be received before such an election can take place, as the Indians of the St. Peter's band are not legally entitled to an election, the elective system, under section 93 of the Indian Act, not having yet been applied to that band by order in council.
3.	Although,. as stated in answer No. 2, the elective system has not been applied to the St. Peter's band, those Indians have been allowed to hold an election every three years. Consequently, the last election having been held on 4th of July, 1905, the present term would naturally expire on 4th of July of the present year (1908).
4.	NO ; as the surrender has already been taken.
5.	On the 16th of January, 1908. the Indian commissioner was reminded, with reference to the petition referred to, that the elective system under section 93 of the Indian Act not having been applied by order in council to any Indian band in Manitoba,

the Indians of St. Peters have no legal right to that system, but that on the other hand, as they have for a long time been allowed the privilege of holding an election every three years, they might now consider that they have a moral claim to the privilege ; but that, as it was then five or six months before the usual date of holding the election, there was time for further consideration of the matter.

Before the orders of the day are called I rise to a question of privilege. In a paper published in Quebec, the ' Le Soleil,' which passes to be the organ of the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Passes ?

There is an article published in this paper which I looked upon as humorous but it might he taken seriously by the readers of that paper and to that article I want to call the attention of the House. It is a long article, but to save time X will translate a summary of its contents:	It says that on the motion made
by the leader of the opposition last Thursday which was directed against the Minister of Marine and Fisheries because he is a French Canadian, all the Conservative French Canadian members except one left the House so as not to vote, and it would imply that they left because they dissented from the motion of the leader of the opposition. The article also says that I spoke upon the question although I did not vote. I want to say that I did not vote because I was engaged outside of the House, but I was paired with my hon. friend from Belle-chasse (Mr. Talbot) and if I had been here I would certainly have voted for the amendment of the leader of the opposition.
I am glad the hon. gentleman from Beauharnois brought this matter to the attention of the House because I intended to do so myself when I had the article translated.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman
rising to a question of privilege ?

Yes, the same question of privilege as that brought up by the hon. member for Beauharnois. The article says that X also shirked the vote because an attack was made on Mr. Brodeur as being a French Canadian and that therefore I did not want to vote. I have to say that I did not vote because I did not want to vote, but at the same time I want to say that I have no belief in the statement that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was attacked because he is a French Canadian. I certainly disapprove of the article in ' Le Soleil.' Here is a paper which is trying to raise a racial cry in the province of Quebec

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman Is proceeding to criticise the general course of a newspaper and that is hardly a proper subject for discussion on a question of privilege.
I have pointed to the allegation in the article and I desire to state my position.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: What is the question of privilege that the hon. gentleman desires to speak to.
The question is that the article is false and I want to show it is.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There must be something personal to the hon. member in his capacity as a member of the House to entitle him to speak to a question of privilege.

My name is twice mentioned in the article and that makes it personal. I wish I had the article here so that I could read it to the House.
I think I have the right to bring to the attention of the House any attack made by a newspaper or any campaign made by any newspaper in any part of the country. This newspaper has been trying to raise racial prejudices

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not taking the proper course to discuss a question of this kind. If there has been something said which the hon. member thinks reflects upon him and which he desires to explain or controvert or deny, he is quite within his rights in discussing that as a question of privilege, but he cannot in this way proceed to discuss the attitude of a newspaper on any question.
The hon. member admits it.
I thought I could explain a newspaper article in which I was referred to by name.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There seems to be at times quite a misapprehension in the House as to what a question of privilege is.
Therefore I do not know when I can bring the question before the House, if it is not a question reflecting on a member.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Going into Supply.
' Le Soleil ' accuses you of not voting and you admit it.
I said I did not vote.
It said you shirked the vote and you admit it.
I admitted that I did not vote.

Speaking on the question of orivilege, I understand that I am mentioned in ' Le Soleil ' in practically the same manner as my hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron). I do not often read ' Le Soleil ' because I find it contains news generally three weeks old, but if I am so mentioned I desire' to express my protest. I was paired that evening with my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Black) and I do not take much stock, and I do not think any one in my province does, in this racial question or the racial character of the attack on the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, because it is too ridiculous.

I also wish to speak on a question of privilege and I am sure tlie House will agree that if I can deny successfully the statement made by the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Commee) I am justified in rising at this time. I am not objecting to any reasonable criticism of that hon. gentleman, but when he accuses me openly on the records of misleading the House, I think that is too serious to pass without comment. In his concluding words the hon. gentleman said :
Now, I think thap my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) did not do himself credit, I do not think he advanced his standing in this House or in the country, by the course which he pursued this afternoon in one particular. He repeatedly stated that the revising officer was a servant of the Ross government, an appointee of the Ross government.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly object to that statement and In order to justify myself in the eyes of the House, the country and of my hon. friend from Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Conmee), who I am sure will be able to set the matter right, I shall relad what I did say. At page 8209 of ' Hansard ' I said :
Now I will refer to the result of that appeal. ' The appeals were directed against 513 names, and instead of having the senior judge of the district to perform his usual functions with regard to those appeals, we had a board of* two. You see the sinister motive of that. Instead of having one judge whose duty had been for years to revise these lists, who knew the law, who knew what the qualifications were, who knew all the tricks of getting men on the list and making an improper list, who was the one man who was competent to sit on these lists, this government deposed him and got two. And why two? So that in case of a disagreement the names should stand on the list. That is the law. If Judge O'Connor differed with the police magistrate with regard to the right of John Jones to be on the list, and the judge said he had no right to he there, and the magistrate said he had a right to be there, he is there, and his name remains on the list.
I do not think I could have put the matter more fairly or more fully. I thought that I had occupied sufficient time to make myself plain, and I strongly protest against being accused, under those circumstances, of misleading the House in that particular.

Mr. R, L. BORDEN. Before the orders of the day are called, I beg to make an inquiry of thf government respecting two statements which I cannot quite reconcile. On the 1st of April the Prime Minister, referring to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, made this statement:

speechtext: In the absence of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries I can only say that I understood it to be the case that Mr. Gourdeau had tendered his resignation and had asked for superannuation. Might I ask what policy is being pursued in the matter of appointing police magistrates or persons to carry out the law against the sale of liquors along the line of the eastern extension of the Grand Trunk Pacific ?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: I am not sure whether that would come under my department or under the Justice Department.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand the inquiry to be what provisions have been made for the enforcement of the prohibition of the sale of intoxicating liquor along the line of the Transcontinental Railway. In reply I have to say that at some period-I am not certain as to the time, but more than twelve months ago-a proclamation was issued covering the strip of territory on either side of tbe line from Quebec to Winnipeg, through the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba. Mr. W. A. Quibell was appointed police magistrate for the portion of that territory extending from Winnipeg to the boundary between Ontario and Quebec. Mr. Lucien Pacaud was appointed police magistrate for the portion of that strip through the province of Quebec. Subsequently, upon the construction of the line between the Quebec bridge and Moncton being undertaken, a similar proclamation was issued constituting a belt of territory. I think ten miles in width, on either side of the line from the south shore -of the St. Lawrence, to the city of Moncton, a territory within the provisions of the statute. The same gentleman, Mr. Pacaud, was appointed magistrate for so much of that belt as is within the province of Quebec. Recently the appointment has been made of a third police magistrate for the portion of that belt in the province of New Brunswick. The gentleman appointed is Mr. Farris, of White's Cove, New Brunswick.
Has that police magistrate the power to try any other cases except in connection with the sale or distribution of liquor?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot reply categorically without referring to his commission. My impression is he has all the powers of two justices of the peace.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman to bring down the commission?
Will the Minister of Railways bring down one of these commissions? That will give us the power.
I will bring down a copy.
Do they sell liquor on the Intercolonial Railway?

The Intercolonial Railway does not sell liquor. One of the difficulties, so other railway companies tell us, in managing the cafe department of the Intercoloniaf Railway, is that all others make a large profit out of that part of their business while the Intercolonial Railway does not sell liquor and is consequently deprived of that profit.

Has the Minister of Militia made any progress in connection with the request made to him by the Prime Minister and supported by myself in respect to the war veterans of Canada having representations at the Tercentenary celebration at Quebec?

speakeroldname: Mr. JAMES CONMEE (Thunder Bay and Rainy River).
speechtext:
At six o'clock yesterday I was making some remarks with respect to the Bill before the House, and I may refer for a moment to the remarks which have fallen from the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce). He thinks that in the remarks I passed upon him yesterday he was somewhat misrepresented. I desire to say that I had no intention of misrepresenting him, and I thought that I stated fairly his position, and it is within the judgment of the House as to whether the remarks I made were quite justified. The hon. gentleman throughout his speech referred to the revising officer as Mr. Quibell. He mentioned the name of the judge on two occasions- one when he read the order appointing the

enumerator, and again when I asked him if Judge O'Connor was not one of the enumerators. Generally speaking the hon. gentleman, whether he noticed himself doing so or not, did refer to the revision being entirely in the hands of Mr. Quibell, and when an hon. gentleman opposite said: 'An official of the Ross government,' my hon. friend assented. Under those circumstances I do not think that the remarks I made were out of place. But I do not wish to tie the hon. gentleman down to that. I am quite willing to accept his explanation that such was not his intention.
Does the hon. gentleman think that anything I said warranted his accusation that I had misled this House?

I think so. I am in the judgment of the House as to that. I do not say that my hon. friend did it intentionally, but that was the impression his remarks gave me, and if any one is responsible, it is my hon. friend. I wish to say that Judge O'Connor, who was appointed revising officer in my hon. friend's riding, is the junior judge of that district, and Mr. Quibell was associated with him in that revision. As these courts are so conducted throughout Ontario, both officers sit together at times. My ho::, friend shakes his head. It is quite possible that in the hurry of the election to which he refers they divided the work. But .1 say that, generally speaking, they sit together.

Will lhy hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) allow me a moment ? I can set him right, I think. It is under the manhood registration Act that there is a board of appeal judges, but under the Ontario Voters' List Act there is only one appeal judge, and that is the district judge.
Unless two are appointed.
They are appointed by statute, the district judge is persona designata under the statute.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) is speaking of the Ontario Act.
Of course, that is the Act I was speaking of.

But this was not under the Ontario Act, this was under the Dominion Act. I am not going to argue whether my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) is technically correct or not ; I am dealing with the impression given me by the language of the hon. gentleman, and I am in the judgment of hon. members as to whether I understood his remarks or not. I do not think mv hon. friend has any complaint to make with regard to Judge O'Connor. Judge O'Connor is a Conservative. I think he is a competent man to conduct such a revision. I think also that Mr. Quibell is a competent man to conduct such a revision. I do not think the hon. gentleman has made out Mr. CONMEE.
a case against either of these officers. The hon. gentleman found fault on the ground that Judge Johnston had not been made a revising officer while Mr. Quibell was appointed to that duty; and he said that Mr. Quibell was an appointee of the Ross government, the inference suggested being that he was a partisan more or less.	My answrer is that, if the hon.
gentleman will canvass his own town of Sault Ste. Marie, he will find that the majority will say that Mr. Quibell is less partisan than the hon. judge to whom he made reference. Mr. Quibell, who has been referred to, was not an official in the ordinary sense of the word. He was a police magistrate, and therefore quite a competent person to be appointed to the position of revising officer.
Now let me point out to my hon. friend the difference between the system followed by the Ross government, and the Liberal government, when in power, and that followed by the present government of Ontario. I made some complaints yesterday of the manner in which the voters' lists are now being prepared in the riding which I represent in this House. The course follow'd by the previous government was to appoint as enumerators in charge of making up the lists, certain officers,-the sheriffs were appointed, as far as I know, and they are responsible officers. But what do the hon. gentleman's friends in power in Ontario, do to-day ? They do not appoint the sheriffs for this work, but they choose the strongest partisans. My hon. friend talks about ' ward heelers,' meaning thereby, I take it, the most extreme partisans. Well, the most extreme partisan in the town In which I live has been appointed the enumerator. And this gentleman Is the agent of the Conservative candidate, so that the enumerator's office and the office of the Conservative candidate are the same. I have here a newspaper-to be fair I must say that it is a Liberal newspaper, but I give its statement to the House because I believe it to be true. I will not give the name, but it states, concerning this enumerator that he is well known to be very active in politics and is the agent of the Conservative candidate, that his office is the office of the Conservative candidate, that he will not deny that he is the employee or partner of the Conservative candidate and that he is actively advocating the interests of the candidate during the time he is acting as enumerator in the riding.	Of course, I
know, my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) is not responsible for all this, I merely point it out to show the spirit that exists. It is about time, ,1 submit, that some law was passed to correct these evils, some system adopted better than the system we have. If the yesterday's argument of my hon. friend pointed to anything, it was to the fact that the existing Dominion law in regard to the preparation of these lists was defective. He

made out a very strong complaint against it. But, if this is so, I would ask him why he is not prepared to join in improving the law by enacting desirable amendments ?

With the hon. gentleman's permission, I would like to ask a question, as I do not wish to misunderstand him. Do I understand him to say that the enumerator appointed by the Ontario government is an employee or partner of the government candidate there ?
Yes.
And does the hon. gentleman say this from his personal knowledge, or does he merely give what this newspaper says ?
I believe it to be the case.
The hon. gentleman has not read the name. I happen to know the name of the gentleman appointed there ; it is Joseph G. Ashford.

That is right. I am glad the hon. gentleman mentioned it, for I can tell my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) ail about it. Joseph G. Ashford was appointed enumerator, but never acted, never was called upon to act. And why ? Because he is an honest man; he is a Conservative, but a straightforward, honest man. And I stated to some of my friends when Joseph G. Ashford was appointed, ' They will never let him act, for he is not the kind of man the machine can use.' And they never did let him act; they held him back ; they never gave him instructions. One of the enumerators, Mr. Eool, completed his list, and yet Mr. Ashford never got instructions to go on. Later, Mr. Hogarth-I will give the name now-who is employed as book-keeper and office man of the gentleman who has been nominated by the Conservative party, whether he is in partnership with him or not I do not know, has been appointed the enumerator and another man with him, whose name I have not before me, but, in any case, it is not Mr. Ashford. Had Mr. Ashford carried out the work of making these lists, I venture to say there would be no complaint and no occasion for appeal, as he would have done what was fair. But what did they do at Fort William ? If my hon. friend wants to force me into a discussion of this question, I have no objection to discuss it, but I am sure that, when we are through, he will have a worse opinion of his friends in Toronto than he has now. I do not like to mention the names of men who are not here, so I will not give this gentleman's name.-The enumerator appointed at Fort William started out in his work. He was a man that did not have a wide acquaintance, he can hardly be spoken of as a well-known man. Well, the law says that the lists should be posted up at every schoolhouse and every separate schoolhouse, but, in this unorganized territory, there are no schoolhouses-or very few and at great distances apart. In any case the facts are, that this gentleman had posted up his lists, that thirty days had elapsed after he had posted them up and that he had gone out on his second round holding his courts, before any Liberal knew anything at all about it, or had any idea that any lists were being prepared. There were no" advertisements in the papers, no notices that really conveyed the information. When the matter was inquired into it was found that this gentleman had posted up on the door of his residence a notice that he was posting up the lists. Well, nobody thought of going to this man's house to find out. Nobody knew' that he -was the enumerator. Nobody knew that he was doing anything, it was entirely in the dark. That list has been completed a considerable time ago, I have a copy of it. Yet Mr. Ashford never got instructions to go, and why, I leave it to my hon. friend to say. I gave an opinion last night that I did not believe there was an honest intention on the part of the powers that be at Toronto to hold elections in those ridings on the same day, and leave it to my hon. friend to judge what v'as meant by holding back Mr. Ashford and then supplanting him by another enumerator who was clerk and agent of the candidate. What I said yesterday I repeat, that in my opinion they cannot hold the elections on the 8th of June, if they have a proper list. The Liberals are up against this difficulty, that they have either got to accept the lists such as they are with out an appeal, or they have got to run the risk of having the elections thrown over and having by-elections, which always places the party in apposition at a disadvantage. I submit that is not fair, and I submit that that is a justification for this Bill we are considering. This Bill is brought forward in order that there may be proper machinery, that there may not be that haste my hon: friend complained of so bitterly yesterday. He says the Bill provides that the list is to be prepared just as the previous Act did. That is not quite correct. It does say that the preparation of the list may be made by order in council after the writs are issued, but it goes on to say that the order in council may be passed at anj time. Now I submit that if the government are charged with the responsibility of preparing the lists, it is reasonable to assume that they will give proper time. The last time the proceeding was new. I was informed, I do not know how coreetly, that they did not discover that it was necessary to make these lists, that it was not known that certain of the provincial lists would be more than a year old, early enough to afford more time and that it was advisable to have recently prepared lists in order that there might be a fair representation of the electors, and that those who were en-

titled to vote might have an opportunity of voting. Therefore there was perhaps some haste the last time. In the riding I represent, I stated yesterday, that I did not think any revision took place. I find on inquiry that I was mistaken ; there was a revision in the Thunder Bay district, but there was no revision, or no appeal at all events, in the Rainy River district. There is a plank in the platform of the Liberal party dealing with the franchise which I wish to place before the House. That plank, adopted in the year 1893, in convention assembled in the city of Ottawa, reads as follows :
Oppose the Dominion Franchise Act-favour the Provincial Franchise.
That the Franchise Act since its introduction has cost the Dominion treasury over a million of dollars, besides entailing a heavy expenditure to both political parties;
That each revision involves an additional expenditure of a further quarter of a million;
That this expenditure has prevented an annual revision, as originally intended, in the absence of which young voters entitled to the franchise have, in numerous instances, been prevented from exercising their natural rights;
That it has failed to secure uniformity, which was the principal reason assigned for its introduction;
That it has produced gross abuses by partisan revising barristers appointed by the government of the day;	_

I am sorry the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) is not in his seat, for I feel sure that, to use a colloquialism, he has allowed these gentlemen to stuff him with a lot of declarations that they cannot substantiate. Let him appeal to Mr. Meikle for his opinion. The only complaint that Mr. Meikle made was that, from a provincial standpoint, it was too expensive to have annual revisions. But the people of Manitoba are not complaining of the expense ; on the contrary they are satisfied with the law and with the government under which it was enacted. On the other hand, during my visit at Easter I did not find a single Liberal who upheld this Aylesworth Bill, which is introduced to perpetrate such great injustice.

House resumed at eight o'clock.

At six o'clock I was comparing the Franchise Act as it stood on the statute-book prior to the advent of the Conservative administration of Manitoba with the Act as it exists today, and I was also dealing with some objections offered by some of the Liberal members of this House to the provisions of the existing Franchise Act. I have to come all the way down to Ottawa, hundreds of miles from my adopted province, to learn of the serious drawbacks and serious objections that exist in the minds of some of these hon. gentlemen in reference to that Act. It seems very strange that, though session after session of the Manitoba legislature has been held since the adoption of the present Act, on no occasion have the Liberals of that body been noticeably active in offering a single amendment to that Act. Now, it is a poor tribute to the intelligence of the Liberals in the legislature of Manitoba that, if all these grievances and all these faults existed in this Franchise Act, the local members should not have bestirred themselves and have taken at least some action in order to remedy those grievances and those complaints which the Liberals of this House are now making in regard to that Act. On the contrary, the only objection that has been urged, the only fault that has been found so far, has been by a gentleman named Campbell, who represents the constituency that the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows) represents in this House, and he put his foot in it so badly that I do not think that he will try it the second time. He charged that certain names that were struck off at a court of revision were afterwards found on the list

and lie accused the government of being a party to this fraud. But when the original list was produced on the table of the local House it was found that his charge was absolutely without foundation; that the lists had been revised by Judge Ryan at Portage la Prairie, a gentleman who possesses the esteem and the respect of Liberals as well as Conservatives in that province; nobody could impeach that gentleman's honour, and Mr. Campbell had to retract his statement and Apologize to the House.
Now, we are told by the hon. member for Lisgar that the time for making up these lists under the existing law is entirely too short, that there is not sufficient time allowed for registration and not sufficient time allowed for the court of revision. All proclamations, according to the present Act, have to be issued by the 1st of May in each year; these proclamations mentio'n the dates and places where the registration is to be held. Ten days' notice at least must be given by the proclamation before the first court of Revision can sit. They sit for a number of days in each constituency, every facility is afforded at every registration booth, and then at least five days must elapse between the last day of the registration court and the sitting of the court of revision, that is the minimum time. Now, if the Liberals have any grievance whatever, they may select one or two isolated cases where there is a short time given between the last day of registration and the first day of the court of revision. But if you take the ' Gazette ' as published on the 25th April, 1908, you will see that out of 37 rural constituencies in that province, but three provide for less than ten days. Moreover, it is not as essential that there should be so long a time between the courts of registration and revision under our laws as it was under the law which existed prior to 1900, because at that time, as I have pointed out, the registration clerks practically made the lists. Under the present law the registration clerks do merely clerical work, accept sworn declarations and pass them on in the presence of the Liberal representatives at the courts of registration, to be passed upon by the different judges at the courts of revision. Ten days, I say, must elapse before the first court of registration is held, and then after they are over, at least five days must elapse before the first court of revision is held. The hon. member for Lisgar selected an isolated case in the constituency of Springfield, within the Dominion constituency of Selkirk, and he said: Here is a large constituency, and there is only one court of revision provided and that eourf sits six days after the last registration sitting. He left the impression, or endeavoured to leave the impression, that that was the general rule, the general practice, that there were only six days in each constituency of that pro-Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
vinee, and that they only had that time to make an appeal. But I have here the Manitoba * Gazette ' Of April 25, 1908, and it contains all the courts of revision and all the registration courts. X have looked through it and counted the number of days allowed for registration in each individual constituency and the time elapsing between the last day of registration and the first day of the court of revision, and I am going to read to you in each constituency the time elapsing between the two. In the constituency of Arthur there are 8 places for registration. Arthur is a small constituency. Many of those constituencies are small and compact and do not require many registration booths and do not require more than one court of revision. There are eight places to register in Arthur, and the interval between the last day of registration and the first day of revision is 24 days, not 6 days as the hon. member for Lisgar tried to make you believe. Then there is the electoral division of Assiniboia, with 10 places for registration, and 20 days of an interval within which they can get their appeals in. Then there is the constituency of Avondale a small constituency, with 6 places to register in and 24 days of an interval, not 6. Now, here is one where I am willing to admit there may be a grievance. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) may have a grievance, and it is in connection with his own local constituency.
I will point out exactly what occurs there. In the constituency of Beautiful Plains there are 9 places to hold registration courts and there is only 3 days interval between the last day of registration and the first day of the court of revision. But, Mr. Speaker, in that constituency, in the principal town, Neepawa, with only about two thousand of a population, they have three days of registration given them. But the representatives of the Liberal party are present to see every application sworn to and handed in to the registration clerk. They can take the names that they object to and appeal them; they can object to none that are handed in' unless they can prove that the party had perjured himself. There are only three days of an interval, but, as I have said, there is not the necessity for the same length of time for appeal. Now, Sir, I am willing to pledge my word as a member of this House, and I think any colleagues from Manitoba will assist me in saying that, feeling that is one instance in jvhicb there should be more time, we will do our best, acting in concert with our Liberal friends in the province of Manitoba, to have that time extended, and I am confident that oversight, for it is only an oversight, will be rectified. Hon. gentlemen on the other side, because they can show one or two isolated instances in which the time may be a little short for appeal, notwithstanding there is not the same necessity for appeal that there was in the days of the

Greenway regime, hold that up as an example of a grievance, just as if one swallow made a summer.
In the constituency of Birtle, in my own constituency of Marquette, there are six places of registration and twenty-three days interval between the registration court and the court of revision. In Carillon there are eleven places of registration and nineteen days interval between the two courts. In the constituency of Cypress there are twelve places of registration, two courts of revision and there are intervals of nineteen and twenty days. In the electoral district of Dauphin there are fourteen places of registration and twelve days of an interval between the last day of registration and the date of the court of revision, and there are two days of registration in the town of Dauphin. In Deloraine there are. ten places of registration and twelve days of an interval between the two courts. In Dufferin there are fourteen places of registration and thirteen days of an interval. In Emerson there are twelve places of registration and fourteen days of an interval. In Gilbert Plains there are no less than 21 places of registration. Why 1 Because it is a very large constituency with outlying points though not thickly populated ?-and every opportunity is afforded the people to register. There are twenty-one places of registration and sixteen days of an interval before the meeting of the court of revision. In Gimli, in the constituency of Selkirk where there are a large number of those foreigners that the hon. member for Lisgar stated that we, on our part, were most anxious to disfranchise and to prevent from registering, there are no less than twenty registration courts open from May 18 to June 8 and two courts of revision. In this constituency in which so many foreigners are located whom we are so anxious to disfranchise, according to these hon. gentlemen, they have two courts of revision sitting on June 16 and June 23. In Gladstone there are twenty places in which the electors may register and they have eight days of an interval between the two courts ; Hamiota eight places to register and twenty-eight days interval ; Kildonan and St. Andrew's also in Selkirk thirteen places to register and an interval of fourteen days and the most northern court is in township 39 range 3 and there are only fourty-four townships in the whole province. This is within thirty miles of the extreme northerly bounds of the province. In Killarney there are seven places to register and fourteen days of an interval. In Lakeside there are nine places to register and eight days of an interval.
These registration courts are not all held on the one day ?
Not at all. They are held on successive days from May 10 to the end of the month.
So that the people will have a much longer time in which to appeal than the actual interval between the meetings of the two courts.

The people have a chance of appealing for a week prior to these four, five, six or any other number of days as the case may be. In some instances they have upwards of a month in which they can get their appeals in. I am only quoting the minimum time from the last day of the sitting of the court of registration until the first day of the court of revision, but from the first day of the registration they have at least a week longer than the time I have given.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if the order followed by the revision judge is the same as the order followed by the registration clerk ?

I am not quite sure of that. One of the reasons why the interval in Beautiful Plains and one or two other constituencies may appear short is, that, as I understand, it is the intention to have county court judges to act as revising officers without calling in any lawyers whatever and they have found a little difficulty in making the dates to suit their own engagements and therefore there are one or two instances in which there is a shorter time than would otherwise be allowed. In Lansdowne there are twenty-one places of registration and twelve days of an interval between the last day of registration and the first day of the court of revision ; La Verandrye, nine places of registration and thirteen days of an interval ; Manitou, eleven places of registration and seventeen days of an interval ; Minnedosa, eleven places of registration and sixteen days of an interval ; Morden, ten places of registration and twenty-five days of an interval between the last day of registration and the first day of revision ; Morris, seven places of registration and twenty-five days of an interval. In Mountain, a local constituency within the district of Lisgar, there are eleven places of registration and two courts of revision. The hon. member for Lisgar was not fair enough to quote an instance in his own constituency, but he went to the constituency of the hon. member for Selkirk in order to get an extreme case to lend point to his argument. But, he did not take a case within his own riding in which there is a preponderating Liberal vote. There are two courts of revision and fourteen and twenty-one days respectively of an interval between the last day of registration and the first day of revision. In Norfolk, which is in the constituency of Portage la Prairie, there are nine places of registration and the hon. member cannot find fault in this case because there are twenty-eight days between the last day of

registration and the first day of the court of revision. In Portage la Prairie, the town practically, there are three places of registration and fifteen days of an interval in which they can get their appeals in. In Rhineland there are five places of registration and thirty days of an interval ; Rockwood, twelve places of registration and fourteen days of an interval. This is also in the constituency of Selkirk. In Russell there are fourteen places to register and seventeen days of an interval. In St. Boniface, represented by the hon. member for St. Boniface, in this House, (Mr. Cyr) there are ten places of registration and twenty-one days in which to get their appeals in. In South Brandon there are nine places of registration and twelve days of an interval. In Springfield, and this is a case quoted by the hon. member for Lisgar, there are eleven places of registration and six days between the last day of registration and the first day of the court of revision. They have in these eleven places of registration from May 21 until June 6. In Swan River there are eight places of registration and ten days of an interval :	Turtle
Mountain, ten places of registration and thirteen days of an interval ; Yirden, seven places of registration and sixteen days of an interval and these registration clerks sit in their offices from 9 o'clock in the morning until 12 o'clock at noon and from 1 o'clock until 6 p.m. and in the cities they sit after 8 o'clock in order to accommodate the workingmen who cannot lose the time to go and register during the day. So that, of these rural constituencies in only three of them is the interval below ten days as a minimum and it runs all the way from that to thirty days and upwards. I do not think that hon. gentlemen have very much to complain of in reference to the time in which they can get their appeals in.
Now, the hon. member for Lisgar has complained, and, I think unfairly complained about the action that was taken by the clerk of the executive council, I presume, who, with a revising barrister, in 1903, held an adjourned court of revision. The names were printed in order to allow the Liberals an opportunity of fighting or testing the case in the court if they desire to do so and because these names were not allowed to go on the corrected voters' lists he denounced the parties to that action. Let me explain what occurred on that occasion. The judges constituting the registration board appointed sixteen Liberals and nineteen Conservatives and they appointed a very strong and active partisan, Mr. Heap, of Selkirk, to revise the lists in this particular constituency. The commission issued to Mr. Heap limited his jurisdiction to a certain date.
He held his court of revision at the time and place stipulated in the proclamation ; he completed his labours and he then took Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
it upon himself illegally to adjourn the court of revision to another time and place, the time being beyond the date fixed in his commission. He had no authority to act as revising barrister after the date of his commission had expired and he was informed by Judge Walker, chairman of the registration board, that he was acting contrary to law, and judge Walker notified the government that this court of revision was taking place illegally. Some twenty names were put on the list by Mr. Heap after his commission had expired but all of those were not the names of Liberals b5r any means. Mr. Heap held his court of revision contrary to the direction of the judge and the government had nothing whatever to do with it. I have already shown in this House that Judge Walker did not sign the same certificate for these illegal lists that he signed for every other revising court in the province. He did not certify as he did in the case of the others that the list of electors was legal and held under the authority and power of the statute, but he gave a certificate merely stating that these names were added at an adjourned court of revision. These names did not appear on the list on polling day and rightly so and if the Liberals thought they had a case they could have tested it in the courts, but none of them attempted to do so. Now, I regret to say that so many Liberals in this House are ignorant on the question of the Manitoba electoral lists and the reason is that they will not stay in their places in this chamber and listen to the truth. They have whispered into their ears by some of their friends from Manitoba, statements that cannot be substantiated. They have been told, as if it were a practice, that electors have been standing at the door of the coivrt of revision and that when the hour for revision expired by law the revising barrister closed his court and allowed those men to be disfranchised. I challenge them to point to one single partisan act on the part of a single revising barrister. In the case of the court of revision presided over by Mr. Bonner, a lawyer of the city of Winnipeg, it was the judges and not the government who appointed Mr. Bonner. Only a very short time prior to that Mr. Bonner was an ardent Liberal. Mr. Bonner held his court and the law read that he should hold his court up to a certain hour and when the hour expired he took it upon himself to close the court although there were quite a few present, and mark vou it is safe to say that there were not any more Liberals than Conservatives waiting. He did not discriminate against one party or the other and even the ' Winnipeg Free Press' has not had the hardihood^ to accuse Mr. Bonner of having acted in a partisan manner. But, the government of Manitoba have taken precautions that such a thing shall not occur again. The

prme minister of Manitoba has time and again invited the Liberals to point out any defects in the law or to suggest any improvements and that he was ready to place on the statute-book any thing that would improve the election law or that would meet any contingency that could possibly arise. The government did not approve of Mr. Bonner's action in interpreting the law so strictly and at the very nest session they brought down this amendment:
The registration clerk shall receive all applications of electors for registration, the striking off of names of electors from the list and for the correction of names on the list, who are present for that purpose at the time fixed for the conclusion of the registration sittings, notwithstanding that such applications are in point of fact received by the registration clerk after the hour of closing the registration sittings aforesaid.
Therefore, if the time arrives for the closing by law of the registration court and there are any electors present the law compels him now to prolong his sittings until each and every one of those present has the privilege of registering, and a similar provision applies to the court of revision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What statute is that ?
I am not certain whether it is the amendment of 1904 or the amendment of 1903.
Did the hon. gentleman complete the reading of that clause ?
I read it to the end and I will read it again. This appeared in the ' Manitoba Gazette ' of February the 20th, 1904.
Where do you find that provision with regard to the court of revision ;

I have not the section at hand now but I will find it. I therefore say that if the Liberals had any grievance in reference to Judge Bonner's court of revision that grievance cannot occur again, and that was the only isolated case that occurred in connection with the revision of the lists throughout Manitoba. That was several years ago and no fault has been found with the annual revision since.
I repeat, that last session the prime minister of Manitoba told his opponents that if they had any suggestions to make in reference to the perfection of the present law he would be only too willing to adopt such suggestions, and yet not an amendment was brought in by a single member of the Liberal party in Manitoba. I am afraid the Prime Minister is not being well informed by his supporters in this matter. Let him apply to Hon. Charles Mickle, leader of the opposition in yie local legislature, who is on record as having stated that our present
lists in Manitoba are the cleanest we ever had in that province.
In what year did Mr. Mickle make that statement ?

About two or three years ago, and our law has been very much perfected since then. He was twitted with it in the legislature not later than last session and had nothing to retract, the only fault he found was the expenditure from a provincial point of view involved in the annual revision. But, as I said, the people of Manitoba do not begrudge a fair expenditure on their voters' lists, in order to have it purged from dead men, non-existant individuals and those not qualified to be on the list. Here is the section that I wish to quote to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, section 11 of the Maui-. toba Elections Act, chapter 52 :
The revising officer shall also receive and deal with the applications of all persons to be registered as electors who shall be present at the time fixed for the closing of the court of revision notwithstanding that the time so fixed shall have elapsed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is that the statute of 1904 ?

This is the Manitoba Elections Act, chapter 52, with all amendments down to 1906. Hon. gentlemen opposite were trying to harp on the question of the hours during which the booths were open simply because there was an isolated case of trouble in connection with Mr. Bonnar's court of revision. There the hours are set and the appeals are necessarily few when every man who wrongfully gets his name on the list must commit perjury to do so. If the hours are not long enough they are extended by the statute I have just read. The hon. member for Lis-gar (Mr. Greenway) has stated that there are many names on the list that should not be there, and that many names that should be there were omitted, but he failed to mention any of these names. He was challenged to do so by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). He stated that he had been in that province for 30 years and knew almost every individual voter and yet he could not name a man who had been left off the list in his own constituency or one who had been improperly placed on it. He was going to do so but failed, and if he were here I would challenge him again to name one individual wrongfully left off or placed on the list. If he gives such a name we will find out whether or not he is correct.
The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows) struck a mare's nest. He thought he had discovered three names that had been put on the wrong form and which the judge stated were names of qualified electors, adding that he was not going to allow any legal technicality to interfere with their

franchise. He thought if he could only show that these three were put on wrongfully, his case had been proved.

The fact is that when these names were objected to the judge asked the Liberals if the men had been notified that they were to be objected to. On being answered in the negative, the judge said they were illegal, but that he could not strike them off without notice.

The judge asked the Liberal representative if they were qualified electors, if they were entitled to vote, and the Liberal representative had to admit that they were. Then said the judge, I am not going to see the men disfranchised, I waive all formalities. But who was to blame for putting them on the list ? The registration clerk did not put the names on the list, he took their declarations handed in by Mr. Parker, transferred them to the revising barrister and Judge Prudhomme put the names on the list. If anything is wrong they must blame the county court judge, the very men whom they want to revise the list under the present Bill. It seems very strange that names could be improperly placed on or omitted from the lists. Where were the Liberals 1 They had the privilege of having representatives at the revision booths. Their representatives were there, every one who was put on had to hand in an affidavit. How did they come to allow these men to hand in false affidavits ? Why did they not appeal and have them struck off. The statements are ridiculous and the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) was indulging in generalities, he could not give a specific case.
But the hon. member for Lisgar excelled himself when he found fault with the qualifications under the present Franchise Act of Manitoba. He said :	I take my stand
as against insisting on 12 months' residence in Manitoba before allowing a man to vote. Consistency thou art a jewel! Who placed the qualification upon the statute ? The Conservative government went out of power in 1888. Under them 6 months' residence in the province and one month in the local constituency was all that was required. The hon. member kept that on the statutes of the province until 1894. He assumed office in December, 1888, but maintained those' qualifications up to the year 1894, and when I find in the statutes of Manitoba of that year, an Act to amend the Manitoba Elections Act, assented to March 2, 1894.
Seotion 12 of chapter 49 of the Revised Statutes of Manitoba, being the Manitoba Election Act, is hereby amended by striking out paragraph (d) thereof, and by substituting therefor the following:
(d) who is, at the date of the issue of the proclamation appointing the registration clerk and has been for three months

Not one month

-immediately prior to the said date, a resident of and domiciled within the said electoral division and has been for one year immediately nrior to' said date a resident of and domiciled within the province.
Not six months as he found it when he came into power, and this is the statute that has been on the statute-book ever since, this is the law that exists to-day ; it has been perpetuated by his successor, and yet the hon. member, forgetful no doubt in his old age of what he did when he was Prime Minister of Manitoba, comes here and condemns the provision requiring 12 months residence in the province.
The hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Bole) is also out of his seat. Well, he is seldom in his seat but when he does come I am very sorry he does not acquit himself a little more creditably than he did on the occasion of his last speech. He devoted a considerable portion of his time to quotations, read, ing some unpronounceable names and affidavits, which affidavits bear on their face the impress of untruth. I am surprised that the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Bole) who has always been looked upon as a respected resident of that city, should come up here and read those affidavits. He even expressed regret that he was forced to do so by reason of the fact that he was a representative of the city. He gave that as an excuse for reading a lot of untrue and scurrilous evidence against residents of Winnipeg who are eminently respectable- evidence intended to smirch their character. By this evidence these men of high repute are accused of having been accomplices in fraudulently putting on names on the voters' lists or causing to be secured false naturalization papers and having them rushed through the county court for the purpose of naturalizing Galicians and other foreigners, not in the country long enough to take out their naturalization papers, thus implicating the clerk of the court in the fraud. While on the one hand he contends that these are the very people the Conservatives want to disfranchise, on the other he trots out those spurious'affidavits in order to prove that the Conservatives were so anxious to get their names on the voters' lists that some of the Conservative officials even descended to making themselves accomplices in this wrong doing. I caught one name-the name of Rudneski. I had heard that name before. I had met the gentleman bearing that distinguished name. At one time he was associated with the Conservative party as a worker among his fellow countrymen. While with the Conservatives, I never heard that he had been guilty of any wrong doing. He was then engaged in legitimate work. But no sooner did he sell his services to our opponents than his descent began in the moral scale. What do we find ? I knew that he had been accused in Win-

nipeg by his fellow countrymen and in my own constituency of some very grievous wrong-doing. The story was circulated in Marquette when he went among his countrymen to help in the Conservative cause- the story was circulated by the Galicians who supported the Liberal candidate, that prior to coming to this country this man had been guilty of wife murder in his own country. I do not know whether there was any truth in that story or not, but that is what his own fellow countrymen said against him. I am not going to vouch for the accuracy of it.
Hear, hear.

But here is something that X will vouch for. I know, as a matter of fact, from reputable citizens of Winnipeg, that he has been guilty of crimes something like those for which Philip Wagner was convicted, that he has defaulted his countrymen right and left, that cases have proceeded against him, that he has been in jail accused even of forgery, and that to-day he is a criminal who has fled this country. In order to refresh my memory and have something to substantiate my statements, I telegraphed to Winnipeg to Mr. Rogers, who was acquainted with that gentleman.
He is not a very good authority.

He is just as good as the hon. gentleman. If the hon. gentleman, who makes sneering reflections upon him, bore as good a character himself, he-would not be quite so ready to interrupt. It is not likely this telegram would be sent me by Mr. Rogers unless there was truth in it. I will read it for the edification of the hon. gentleman and his colleagues.
Winnipeg, May 7, 1908. To W. J. Roche, M.P., Ottawa.
Rudneski served considerable time in the common jail here. Had to skip the country last year.
Is there anything in that which the hon. gentleman can contradict ? If so I would like to hear it.
Rudneski made by himself and others eight affidavits and sold the .same to George Walton, Liberal organizer, for $25. I hold the original oheque.
Does the hon. gentleman dispute that ?-
I hold the original cheque given by Walton to Rudneski in payment of those affidavits. The same will be published in to-night's paper. The original cheque will be mailed you at Ottawa. Do not lose cheque as I want to get it cashed some day. Affidavits from all the parties named by Bole or Rudneski will appear in to-night's or to-morrow's paper to show that statements made by Bole or Rudneski are absolutely false. Insist on Bole
reading the other five affidavits for which Rudneski was paid by Liberal organizer.

These hon. gentlemen thought they had discovered something fine when they trotted out those affidavits made by those Galician residents of Manitoba. But anyone reading them would see that they bore on their face the impress of untruth. Here is something that will appear in the public press of Winnipeg to-morrow ; and if Mr. Walton finds he has a libel action, he will have the opportunity to enter the courts against the author of that telegram or the authors of the affidavits published in the city of Winnipeg. This is the character of the evidence which has been read in this House in order to try and influence the Prime Minister and his associates and induce them to inflict upon us this Aylesworth Bill calculated to deprive the Conservatives of Manitoba of their franchise. Why the very thing incorporated in those affidavits, the charge of illegally naturalizing hundreds of foreigners who are not long enough in the country, is the very thing these hon. gentlemen themselves were guilty of at the last election. If my memory serves me correctly, we had some of those men in court for having got some of the poor deluded Galicians, who were not long enough in the country to understand our laws, our custom^, our institutions, out language-for having got them naturalized and they had to answer for that in the court. When I was at home during the Easter holidays the very thing they accused us of having done in these by-gone days is what I heard they were doing very recently throughout the Galician colony. They were getting out naturalization papers, getting blanks signed in some cases, getting these foreigners to sign affidavits of the contents of which they were ignorant, so that the very thing they charge against the Conservatives in those spurious affidavits, they are doing themselves at present.
It seems to me very strange that this provincial law, which is held up to so much odium, is the law which the Minister of Justice says he follows out in its entirety' in the revision of the lists as provided for in his own Bill. After denouncing the provincial law as unfair in every particular, they are going to follow it in its entirety. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) also referred to another matter, and I marvel at his ingratitude. He referred to the placing on the lists the names of some seven electors who had been left off the lists at one time. But before going further, I wish to say further in connection with the Rudneski affidavit.
It seems strange, as the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) stated, that this affidavit should be in possession of the hon. member (Mr. Bole) for twelve months and
revised edition

that lie should wait until he got to Ottawa aud read it in this House in order to prejudice members against the law existing in his own province. Mr. Walton, the Liberal organizer, the gentleman accused in this telegram of having bought these affidavits for $25 had not the manliness, or rather I should say he was too manly, to utilize them.' And he is a member of the legislature and was there during the recent session, yet he did not mention or read these affidavits in the legislature where he could be met by the premier, and others who are in possession of information to controvert them. He could not do it; he was ashamed to. I have no doubt he felt that this was $25 wasted. But he transferred these affidavits to the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Bole), who is now a resident of Montreal, and is not to receive renomination in his present constituency, that that hon. gentleman might do work to which Mr. Walton would not stoop to do in connection with his legislative duties.
Now, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) spoke about the Balsam Bay electors. He said, referring to the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) :
X. The hon. gentleman said that this Manitoba government which takes such care of the voters was good enough upon one occasion to solemnly pass an Act of parliament to place certain individuals upon the list in order that they might vote. And now, I come to a discussion of the 'thin-red-line.' We are not afraid to discuss this, as the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) seemed to think we should be. What does the ' thin-red-line ' mean ? The voters' lists sent by the clerk of the Crown in Chancery to the various returning officers in Manitoba previous to the last Dominion election were mutilated, and mutilated illegally, and scores and hundreds -how many it is impossible to say*-of Conservatives were disfranchised by Leach and his associates through the mutilation of these lists. Now what had they to do ? The Dominion Act provides that where there is an overlapping of constituencies the returning officers should have power to divide the lists, but only in those places, and in no places in the interior. That is the Dominion Act, section 25, and I will read it:
Where any provincial polling division, as constituted at the time of the receipt by the returning officer of the writ for an election lies only partly within the electoral district for which such election is to be held, the part thereof within such electoral district shall, for the purpose of that election, form a separate polling division, or it may be attached by the returning officer to an adjoin-255$
ing polling division, and the returning officer shall, as soon as possible after the receipt of the writ, prepare from the existing voters' lists a separate voters' list containing the' names of the persons entitled to have their names placed on the list for such part of such polling division.

Of the two voters who marked their ballots in favour of the Liberal candidate one afterwards admitted that

he had marked his ballot in mistake for the Liberal candidate. The other ballot was marked by a gentleman from Toronto who came in at the last hour to cast his vote and had not time to go to a more distant poll. Of these eighteen ballots, sixteen were marked in favour of the Conservative candidate, one was inadvertently marked in favour of the Liberal candidate and one voter had to mark his ballot as an agent of the candidate. That would have been shown to have been prevalent at many polls if we had had the time and the opportunity to prove it, and if we had had the assistance from this government that we were entitled to have, they being responsible for the prosecution of these cases.
What reason or pretence of reason was assigned for interfering with the lists in polling divisions which were wholly within the boundaries of a federal electoral district ?

There was absolutely no reason or pretence whatever except that these gentlemen thought they had a perfect right to go on and mutilate the lists without warrant, and they had no warrant at all. The Dominion Election Act provides that they shall adopt the provincial polling subdivisions. I have here the Act. The Dominion Election Act, chapter 6, section 24 provides that:
The polling divisions shall, except as herein otherwise provided for, be those established by or under the laws of the province for the purposes of provincial elections within the territory comprised in the electoral district tor which the eleotion is held.
So, in the face of the statute these returning officers, or at least, Mr. Leach, acting on behalf of the returning officer, mutilated, divided up, carved up the lists for the province of Manitoba notwithstanding that the provision of the statute is that they should adopt the provincial polling subdivisions. Had they adopted the provincial polling subdivisions there would have been no ground for complaint save in these border constituencies, and I have no doubt that matters could have been arranged to the satisfaction of everybody. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford) says that there was no complaint in his riding. Why ? Because Mr. Leach did not mutilate the lists. He did not transfer the names ; they had a returning officer who did that work and if what the hon. gentleman states is correct, I presume he did it iho.nourably. We are told there were piio complaints in Brandon and elsewhere, and why ? Mr. Leach himself swore he did not touch either of these constituencies. It is only where the returning officers handed over their lists to the Liberal organizer, and this is significant and certainly not accidental- it is in these cases that the lists were work-Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
ed to the destruction of the Conservative electors and to the disfranchisement of no doubt hundreds of voters in that province. No better argument could be used as to there being no necessity whatever for interference with the present provincial law than this very fact. Had the returning officers discharged their duties, as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie says his returning office did, there would have been no ground for complaint. If these polling subdivisions overlap they might have an opportunity there of getting in their funny work, but had the government itself in that instance followed out the law as it is in Manitoba to-day there need be no trouble in that respect.
Was not this matter of the cutting and carving of the lists in the polling subdivision passed on by the Court of Appeal in Manitoba?
Yes, I will deal with that in a moment.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) whether or not any notice was given to the Conservative candidates or organizers when the lists were being mutilated in this way?

No, absolutely no. And where Liberals were transferred they took mighty good care they sent out information to them in order that they might know where, to vote, while the Conservatives were absolutely ignorant of the fact until election day, and even then they were unable to find out where they were transferred to. And while throughout Manitoba there were a large number- no doubt hundreds, but how many it is impossible to say-absolutely disfranchised by reason of being left off their lists and by reason of being taken off their own polling subdivision and not transferred to any other, still there were a greater number who were disfranchised by reason of their being transferred to other lists, 10 or 15 or 20 miles from their own home so that they did not know where to vote.
The Minister of Justice stated he was quite confident that there were not more than 100 disfrachised in the province of Manitoba. It is strange that we who reside in Manitoba have to come to Ottawa to learn that from the Minister of Justice. I certainly would not undertake to vouch for the number of electors that were disfrachised ; I do not think I could come mithin several hundreds of the number if I made a guess, but the Minister of Justice sitting down in Ottawa knows all about it and he can tell almost to a man the number who were disfranchised. How he can make such a statement as that is past my comprehension. No doubt he got his information from his supporters who know just as little about it as he does. I have

here a facsimile map of the vote held at Beausejour at poll No. 9. This map is marked in sections and the * X ' on the section represents the names left on the list and the * O ' represents the names taken on.
