Does any one suppose that was accident? If they say it was by accident they may tell it to the marines. No intelligent man will believe it. There does not seem to be any particular method in striking off the names except the method of selecting the Tories and taking them off the list. I will pass this around for the inspection and information of hon. gentlemen, so that they may see that on one section of land there would be four residents, two of them Liberals and two of the Conservatives, two transferred, two not transferred-and those that were disfranchised were the two Conservatives. Can the Prime Minister uphold such a thing as that? I am sure his supporters have not told him one-half the nefarious transactions in the holding of that election. Well, these officials were arrested and after the preliminary investigation they were sent up for trial. At the first trial the judge threw out the charge on the technical ground that the words ' wilfully erased ' were not inserted in the charge, and he stated that had to be proven, and so a different procedure had to be taken. It came before Judge Perdue and Judge Perdue after hearing counsel withdrew it from the jury again on technical grounds as to what constituted a voters' list. An appeal was taken from Judge Perdue's decision and it came before' the full court consisting of Judge Kichards and Judge Phippen. I told in my hand the judgment of the full court, and I will read it to the House. This is it:
When the returning officer appointed to hold a Dominion election for an electoral district in Manitoba, selects one of the copies of the lists of voters sent to him by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery pursuant to section 21 of the Dominion Elections Act 1900, as the one which he will certify and forward to the deputy returning' officer as required by section 41 for use at one of the polling subdivisions, that copy so selected becomes a voters' list within the meaning of section 503 of the Criminal Code 1902, and it is an offence under that section for the returning officer wilfully to erase names of voters from it, either before or after he certifies it and forwards it to the deputy.
That was the point on which Judge Perdue withdrew the case from the jury.
Such returning officer has no authority under the Dominion Elections Act, 1900, to create a voters'list upon which the election is to be held, or, under sections 22 and 23 of the Elections Act to make a new division of a constituency into polling subdivisions and rearrange the names of the voters for each when there are
in fact polling divisions already established and used at the last provincial election for the same territory, whether or not such polling divisions had been erected in strict accordance with the requirements of the provincial statutes. The returning officer who wilfully makes such erasures from the voters' lists cannot escape punishment on the ground that he had to make them in consequence^ of having made new polling subdivisions which he had no authority to make. The fact that the heading of the list of voters in question used the words 'registration district No. 3,' instead of ' polling division No. 3 ' did not justify the returning officer in believing, if he did believe, that there were no polling divisions, since the territory of No. 3 was correctly described in the same heading.	_	_
The court having held that the trial judge had erred in withdrawing the case from the jury and directing a verdict of not guilty, ordered a new trial. .
There is the court of appeal distinctly pointing out that this returning officer had no business whatever to violate the Dominion Elections Act in the manner in which he did. If they had complied with the law there was no possible justification or excuse for adopting the method of dividing the list in order to conform to this new policy of subdivisions. I would read a few words from the argument that followed. Judge Richards stated :
The contention for the defendant is that, under section 22 of the Dominion Elections Act, a returning officer is required or permitted to fix the limits of polling divisions, and necessarily therefore to deal with the lists of voters sent him by the clerk of the crown in chancery by so altering them that they shall suit the limits of the divisions that he so fixed.	.
I find myself unable to accept that view. Section 22 only requires, I think, that returning officer to get the documents or papers (other than voters' lists) named in that section, for the purpose of ascertaining what the already established polling divisions are.
Further on, Judge Richards said:
It was admitted by defendant's counsel on the argument that the defendant did in faot, by his proclamation under section 16, alter the area of the polling division to which the list which he is charged with altering applied. He took off part of the area and. added territory not previously in the division.
It was argued that, even if he had done that wrongly (as it seems to me that he did) it, nevertheless, became necessary as a result of that alteration that he should alter the list so as to make it correspond with the new limits, and that such latter alteration thereto became his duty and that as a result he could not lie punishable for making it wilfully, but that his only liability, if any, would be for the alteration of the area of the. division.	,	,
The contention, if sound, would imply that, because he committed a breach of the law, which he should have known would necessarily cause him to commit a further breach, he is not to be responsible for committing the

second breach. If that were good law, then if statutes forbid changes in the divisions and also forbid changes in the lists, but provided penalties for the latter offence only, a returning officer who wished to alter the lists to favour a candidate could do so with impunity by first deliberately altering the divisions and then justifying under such last named alterations when charged with having changed the lists.
, Where a man commits a breach of law knowing that it will necessarily involve his committing another breach, and he does also commit that other breach, it seems to me that to the extent to which the law provides penalties for such breaches he is liable to punishment for either, or for both of them.
In this he was supported by Judge Phip-pen iu the following words :
It is now argued that the returning officer may disregard these conditions and of his own judgment, under section 23 of the Dominion Elections Act, declare ' that under the laws of the province there are no polling divisions for the purpose of provincial elections/ and then proceed to create divisions and prepare new lists.
I do not think the statute will bear any such construction. To my mind parliament never intended returning officers, appointed and acting in the heat of an election, to be the final court of appeal and to determine such delicate matters in the absence of the parties and with no provision for their being heard. Such questions can be settled only by the courts, then all parties will at least have an opportunity of being present. There were polling divisions in fact for the purpose of provincial elections, and beyond that the returning officer had no authority to inquire. It was not his business to reject that which in fact existed because of supposed illegality in its creation. I am, however, inclined to the opinion that these polling divisions were such in law as well as in fact.
I would therefore answer the questions stated in the case as follows: In my opinion the learned trial judge did not properly withdraw the case from the jury, nor did he properly direct a verdict of ' not guilty ' to be entered.
There is the decision of the court of appeal and in the face of that the Minister of Justice declared that somebody had to do this dividing, that it was necessary that it should be done, and why then do we condemn them for the operation of the red line ? The provincial government used the black line. Who used the black line ? The judges of the province of Manitoba are commanded by law to make the division where there is overlapping or a new registration requiring the division of the lists. That work by the provincial law is to-day in the hands of the county court judges, any judge to be named by the Lieutenant Governor in Council and to that judge is assigned the duty of making a division. It is not left to any returning officer. Which is the fairest law, the present provincial law leaving this work to the judges or the

proposed law which we are now discussing? In connection with this red line business Mr. E. L. Howell appeared to defend the culprits, R. E. A. Leach and his associates, and he stated that he appeared there on behalf of the Dominion government. Fancy these men, who had been guilty of this act as evidenced by the decision of the court of appeal, who had disfranchised the Conservative electors by the score and by the hundred, being defended by Mr. F. L. Howell, of Winnipeg, who stated that he was there at the instance of the Justice Department of this government. How different were their actions in 1896 when they caused the arrest of a number of innocent deputy returning officers in Macdonald, where there were supposed to be unwarrantable trafficking with the polls and disfranchisement of Liberal electors. Did the provincial government there, although a Liberal government, spend any of their money ? Not at all, they called on their friends here and this government spent nearly $10,000 without securing a verdict against any one of them, in hunting down the supposed criminals. But in this case they sent their legal representative in Winnipeg to defend the culprits who had been guilty of disfranchising their Conservative opponents.
I quoted a while ago the statement that under the provincial law the judges have to do the dividing of the territory and of the lists. Here is the statute for that:
In the event of territory comprised within or partly comprised within an electoral division being changed and included in another electoral division, or other electoral divisions, whether newly created or not, a judge of one of the county court divisions of the province, to be nominated and appointed by the Lieutenant Governor in Council, shall subdivide the names appearing on the list of electors as so finally revised, according to the altered boundaries or limits, and make a complete list of electors for the electoral divisions affected, as aforesaid, and appropriately divide the names of electors and allot the territory between suitable polling subdivisions as shall in the opinion of such judge be just and equitable.
Is that not a fair provision to have the work done by the provincial judge of Manitoba, taking it out of the hands of the returning officers ? By this It is possible to judge which law Is the more fair.
Some returning officers were arrested. One of them was named Duggan-and by the way I cannot congratulate the government on the superiority of the gentlemen whom they selected in some instances at any rate, to act as returning officers. This gentleman's training, however reputable he may be, has not been such as to win the confidence of the electors of that constituency. Mr. Duggan, some time before he was selected, was a clerk in a hotel kept by his brother in Selkirk,
That is not correct.
That is in the evidence, anyway.
It is not.

I think it will be found that I am right. The hon. gentleman once before contradicted me. I referred to Mr. Duggan as a bartender at one time. That statement is not correct.
We will look up the evidence and see whose memory is the best. What was Mr. Duggan?
Go ahead and tell It.
In what capacity was he acting prior to being appointed?
Was he a bartender?
No, he was not.

Q. Did you supply any one with a copy of the lists as altered?-A. No.
Q. Did you show anybody a copy of the lists as altered?-A. No.

That is the lists he received from Mr. Leach.

Here is a returning officer who certified to this list as being correct. In the face of the declaration of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth), who states that there
were not over 100 electors disfranchised iu the whole province of Manitoba, here is a returning officer who swears that there might have been 500 names struck off that list and not put on any other and he did not know anything about it.
Why did the Attorney General of Manitoba enter a nolle prosequi in this particular case?

I am coming to that.
Q. And that is the conclusion to draw from the fact that you did not check them over. You cannot tell whether 500 were disfranchised or not owing to the alterations?-A. I could not swear.
Q. And yet you as returning officer certified to the correctness of the list you issued?-A. Yes.
That is the kind of returning officers this government appointed. Whether there were 100 or 500 disfranchised, they certified to the list without knowing about it, but the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) knows to a man almost how many were disfranchised in the whole province.
Mr. Leach was also sworn. He said at the investigation that he was the chief organizer of the Liberal party.
Give me the names of any men outside of the few who were disfranchised.
Give me the various voters' lists, some of which are here in the office of the clerk of the Crown in Chancery, and give me the lists that were destroyed by your deputies and I will show you.
That is no answer to my question.
I can give the hon. gentleman twenty-eight of them.

I went to the clerk of the Crown in Chancery and asked to be allowed to peruse some of those lists, and he admitted that many had not been returned at all. Where are they? They were destroyed no doubt by the various deputies lest they might be incriminated, and now, four years afterwards, the hon. gentleman challenges us to give the names of the men who were disfranchised.
I am just following your leader's example. He is a great man" for challenging to give names. I will give some to-morrow.

During 1904 Mr. Leach was chief organizer for the Liberal party. In the summer of that year he had been doing organization work in connection with the voters' lists for the Manitoba constituency. He had been doing the work of preparing the lists for the committees, copying in the books the reports, preparing a different division of the polling districts

from those mentioned in the registration papers. Some time before the election and before the writs were issued, he was making arrangements for having the lists in the elections different from those used in the Dominion elections. He was asked:
Q. What were the methods of arriving at the lists which were used?-A. After planning cut what we thought would he suitable polling subdivisions, we prepared lists to conform with these divisions.
Q. Who were present while you were doing that work? I presume you were not personally doing the work yourself? Did you supervise the work?-A. I directed it.
Q. Who were the persons actually doing the work?-A. Mr. Neighorn was chiefly charged with the responsibility.
b He goes on to say that he did not touch either the Brandon, Dauphin or Portage lists. That is the reason these gentlemen had no complaints coming in. Mr. Leach did not have the opportunity of disfranchising in connection with these lists. But with these exceptions, all the lists in the other constituencies were prepared under his supervision. On being asked regarding the secrecy of the operations, he gave evidence as follows :
Q. You Carried out the work in the same way as the rest of the work in this office-in such a way that information as to what was being done did not go outside, as far as you know?-A. It did not get outside.
Q. Except to the Liberal organization and the persons you thought entitled to the information?-A. We did not take any pains to notify our opponents.
Q. But you took good care to keep your work from your opponents. You were doing your work as effectively as possible?-A. It turned out to be effective.
This is the Leach who flaunts the operation of the thin red line as having done its work very effectively in disfranchising the citizens of that province. The Liberal organs of Manitoba have been writing up articles to supply these gentlemen down here with material for this discussion. The authority is a very poor one, but let me give you the very best that the 'Free Press' can say

not that I agree with its conclusions, because I entirely disagree with them, but to show the very best face that can be put upon these proceedings :
Free Pr.ess, February If, 1908.
On the whole the work was done in 1901, in view of the limitations of time, with creditable acouraoy. In practically only three constituencies were there any real grounds of complaint. There were clean lists in Winnipeg, Souris, Dauphin, Marquette, Brandon and Lisgar.
I beg to differ. There were not clean lists in Marquette or one or two other of those constituencies, but where there were clean lists is where Mr. Leach did not have the opportunity of using the red line.

In the constituencies of Macdonald, Selkirk and Provencher there were, in some four or five polling divisions, undoubtedly irregularities.
What a mild term !
Whether these were wilfully done or not has never been established. The points at which names had either been carelessly transferred or unintentionally dropped

As, for instance, where there were 41 names scored off the list 23 of which did not appear on any other list, of which 18 were the names of Conservatives-that was merely ' careless transferring.' Of course, it was quite unintentional-but it was significant just the same.
-were Beausejour, St. Boniface and Miami. There also appears to have been some trouble at Poplar Point, although no attempt has ever been made to state the facts as to these cases.
The article goes on :
It can, however, be said that at the outside not more than forty or fifty parties lost their votes

This was stated by the hon. member for Lisgar and will be stated by other hon. members on that side. This is their authority for that statement.
-'and that with the possible exception of Provencher, the results of the Dominion elections were in no wise affected by these mistakes.
Here is an acknowledgment that a gentleman sits on the Liberal side of this House representing a constituency-Pro-vencher-that was stolen from the Liberal Conservative candidate. Here is the admission of the Liberal party organ that that constituency at least was stolen from the Conservatives. Their candidate had a majority of only 10, and in St. Boniface alone there were 25 Conservatives who were disfranchised, more than double enough to wipe out the Liberal majority. And this is the kind of argument that these hon. gentlemen put up to bolster up their case.
I am just reminded, in connection with the duplicate list, that Mr. Leach swore he was provided with only one copy of these lists by those whom he had in his employ. But he is distinctly contradicted by Neighorn who did the altering of the lists. Leach swore that he left it with Neighorn, and Neighorn swore that he made a duplicate list and handed both to Leach. And, no doubt, the duplicate was sent to his political friends to notify them where they were to go to poll their votes.
Now, I am asked by the hon. member for Pictou, ' Why were these cases dropped ?' What have we read in the Liberal press ever since this question arose in 1904 ? Persecution ! Persecution on the part of the provincial government of Manitoba against these poor officials who had done nothing wrong. So it has been stated, but I do not

think they will state it again. We were told that these officials were being persecuted. They were taken from court to court until they were brought to the court of appeal. And there it was decided that they were wrong, that they had no right to make these new polling subdivisions, and no right to treat the lists as they did. What was the use of going on when there was a decision of that kind, in the face of which "such actions cannot be repeated. Had we gone on, the charge of ' persecution ' would have been hurled still more viciously against the Conservatives. But another reason why these cases were dropped was that the Dominion government had turned this into a political question by sending Mr. E. L. Howard to represent the party in these *cases. Would it be possible to get a jury that would not be a political jury with the Dominion government defending the accused ? X think this is a sufficient answer to the hon. member for Pictou. Had the cases gone on we should have heard much more from the Liberal representatives and the Liberal press the accusation that we were persecuting these returning officers. In fact the Minister of Justice admitted as much by stating that if the present law were left in force, it would be impossible to get men to act as returning officers in future. But, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) rightly stated, that any returning officer who discharged his duty faithfully and well in accordance with his sworn declaration need not fear the law,-if he does his duty he has nothing to fear. Now, why were the lists in the constituency of Selkirk handed to Leach ? Mr. Duggan had been a resident of the constituency for fifteen years, and must have been much better acquainted with the constituency than Leach, in fact, Leach had no local knowledge of the constituency. Mr. Duggan, if he had an education and was a proper man to act in that capacity, having been a resident for so long, should have been able to do the work himself.
Now, what became of these gentlemen ? In the first place, we have Leach appointed to a position by the Minister of the Interior-not the present Minister of Interior. Leach carried on this work for the election in December, 1904. He was in charge of the province of Manitoba as organizer. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) was Minister of the Interior at that time. Mr. Leach was a confidential friend of that hon. gentleman, and, after perpetrating these gross frauds he was rewarded by being appointed to a position under the Crown the salary of which was $3,000, if I mistake not To-day he is on the pay-roll of this government, acting in the capacity of inspector of land offices. Mr. Neighorn, the chief man in charge, has also been rewarded by being made, I believe, private secretary to the chairman of the Transcontinental Commission. Mr. Ayotte, the returning
officer for Provencher, has been rewarded with a place as immigration agent in the United States where he draws a salary the amount of which I have forgotten. He is pensioned upon the people of this country for his services to the Liberal party on that occasion, and McLeod was similarly rewarded with a government position. Each and every one of these men is to-day on the pay-roll of this country; instead of being punished for their nefarious transactions, they have been rewarded by this government in accordance with its well-established practice.
Now, this action of the government in trying to force this Election Act upon us is an evidence, a confession of the pitiable weakness of their position with the western people. As I have already said, the government fear a free and untrammelled verdict of the people. They have placed imposition after imposition upon the little province of Manitoba ever since they came into power. For reasons best known to themselves, they have been punishing that little province until now we have the crowning iniquity of endeavouring to throttle the franchise of that province. I can tell the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that he is not going to improve his reputation with right-thinking people, Liberals as well as Conservatives, by this measure, for it is resented by the people of the west, but especially of Manitoba, irrespective of party. This measure is an acknowledgment that the government cannot hope to carry Manitoba without resorting to loaded lists. Sir, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) when prime minister of the province, ran elections in 1892, 189G, 1899, and he never once ran an election without loaded lists. And to-day, because the lists in that province are absolutely as fair to one party as to the other, that hon. gentleman and his colleagues in this House-every one of whom has sat in the legislature behind him as premier-demand that the same handicap should be placed upon their opponents in Dominion elections.
Talk about the list being unfair. I picked up fio-day the ' Winnipeg Telegram ' and what do I find ? You would not find this in any Liberal organ in any (province of the Dominion of Canada, unless they were perfectly sure of their ground. This paper offers a bonus of $25 for every case that can be found of a man who has been improperly left off the list during this coming revision. The ' Telegram ' offers a bonus of $25 to any man who can substantiate before an impartial judge that he has appeared before a registration clerk in the coming revision this month, or next month, who is qualified to get his name on the list, and who has been refused. And who do they select for the judge ? The Hon. Charles Mickle, leader of the Liberal party in tne local legislature of Manitoba. Here is the 1 article in that paper :

There is not another province in Canada that can show such a record in the administration of its election law. There is no partiality in the administration of Manitoba's election law, for the simple reason that the system makes the elector independent of officials and renders partiality obsolutely impossible. The ' Telegram ' is confident that the fairness and impartiality which have characterized previous registrations in the province of Manitoba will characterize the registration which is about to be held. It is so confident that the electors of the province, irrespective of party sympathies, will be dealt with fairly that it makes the following proposition :
The ' Telegram ' will pay the sum of $25 to any elector in the province of Manitoba who is not already on the voters' lists who is refused registration if he applies in the regular manner and is legally qualified to vote under our law. Should any claim or claims bo made under this offer each case to be referred to Hon. C. J. Mickle, leader of His Majesty's loyal opposition in the Manitoba legislature, from whose decision there shall be no appeal. Should any award be made, one half the amount is to be paid to the elector who has been refused registration and the other half to the Winnipeg General Hospital.
I ask the Prime Minister, is it reasonable to suppose that any person holding a responsible position would make an offer of that kind if he did not feel absolutely sure of his position, absolutely confident that no such case can be found ? Under the existing law both parties will be at the court of revision, each party will have an equal chance with the other, and I say it is absurd to suppose that these charges of unfairness can be substantiated. But that is not all. Information came to me to-day that this offer is going to be followed up by another to the effect that if it can be shown that any elector was unjustifiably kept off the list at the last revision, having complied with the law in every respect, or if he was improperly left off the list, or if anybody was improperly struck off the list -and I desire to emphasize this, because no registration clerk in the province of Manitoba has power to strike a single man off the list the judge may do so, the revising barrister-I believe that to-morrow's ' Telegram ' will say that if it can be shown that any one was disfranchised improperly last year, they will pay $25 for every such case, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself shall he the judge. Now I think our Liberal friends, Instead of indulging in declamations and reckless assertions, should come down to hard facts, and give us specific cases if they are able to do so.
Now it has been stated that in 1904 Mr. Sifton endeavoured to pass an Act similar to this. So he did. The Prime Minister knows that. He knows that an Act was hatched, was printed in fact, but it never saw the light of day so far as this parliament is concerned, strangled almost before Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
it was born, by reason of the fairness of the predecessor of the present Minister of Justice. The present Minister of Justice, "though, will strike an opponent below the belt, he will stoop to do things of this kind that his predecessor in office would not resort to. He came into parliament with a great reputation as a legal authority ; as a politician he has proved a huge failure, hut as a partisan he has proved a splendid success. He is making for himself a reputation that certainly is not enviable west of the great lakes. In 1904, as I say, Mr. Sifton hatched an Act and told his friends never to mind a revision ; I am going to introduce an Act, he told them, that will take the lists entirely away from the officials of the local legislature, and we will have our own officials prepare the lists. It was because of that that the Liberals in Manitoba did not become active in connection with the revision of 1904, and hence they had to resort to the thin red line, they had to make it up iu some way, and they endeavoured to do it by that method. Now what does this Bill provide. There is a very significant clause here, subsection 2, which reads:
In the preparation of such lists the provisions of the laws of the province regulating the preparation and manner of revising and bringing into force the provincial voters' lists in the like oases shall as far as possible

Very significant words in the light of past experience.
-be observed and followed and no person whose name is not included in the voters' lists so prepared and revised shall be entitled to vote.
What do I mean by saying, ' In the light of past experience ? ' We had a by-eleetion in the constituency of Lisgar in 1901. The then representative, Mr. Richardson, was unseated, and a by-election was held in consequence. The provincial voters' lists were upwards of one year old. The Dominion law provides that when the lists are upwards of twelve months old, the Dominion officials shall make up lists of their own, a law with the identical words in it, following as far as possible the provisions of the provincial law. What did they do ? At that time the judges constituted the hoard of registration as they do now, the five judges of the province of Manitoba. These five judges had the power to say where the registration booths should be placed, they had the naming of the registration clerks, they had the naming of the revising barristers, the government had not a single word to say in either of these respects, either in placing the registration booths in the different districts, or in appointing the registration clerks, or in naming the revising barristers. The government had not the slightest thing to do with all that. Did this government follow out

the provision of that law ? They could have done so, but they ignored it. What did the late Minister of the Interior do ? He appointed a gentleman named, I think, Alexander McLeod, a strong Liberal partisan, and they constituted him a board of registration instead of the judges under tlie provincial law. Was that fair towards their opponents ? They ignored the provincial law entirely. Now it was not impossible to have taken these judges as the provincial law required. But they appointed this Liberal lawyer and gave him all the power that the provincial law centred in the judges. He designated where the registration booths should be, and placed them in the most inconvenient places for the Conservatives in that constituency. He appointed the registration clerks every man of whom was a partisan Liberal, and he appointed the revising barristers, not one of whom was a Conservative. These gentlemen claim that under the present Act all the registration clerks are Conservatives. Hoes this Aylesworth Bill provide that there shall be a Tory appointed to revise the new lists ? Do you suppose that it worked a hardship ? Is it wrong to have a Tory appointed as a registration clerk and is it right to have a Liberal ? Alex. McLeod appointed partisans as his officials. The Liberals appointed revising barristers of their own political faith, and they appointed registration clerks, partisans of their own. They ignored absolutely the provisions of the law. Hence, I say these words, ' as far as possible,' are utterly meaningless, and that with the provision of the present Act w'e would just see a repetition of what we did see in connection with the Lisgar election of 1901.
I wish to anticipate one or two things that no doubt will be said and to refer to one or two things which have been said by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford). He made a speech prior to the Christmas holidays in connection with the voters' lists and he made several accusations in connection with the revision of the lists' that are absolutely foundationless, as I have already proved, in connection with the Balsam Bay revision where seven names were left off. At page 348 of ' Hansard ' the hon. member for Portage la Prairie referred to the official voters' list of the district of Rockwood and he complained of the fact that 90 names had been struck from the voters' lists of polling subdivision No. 1 of that district and some 45 names left on. He made the bold statement that if the act had been done by a Grit he would have been put in the penitentiary, but as it was done under Tory instructors every man got scot-free. As a matter of fact the striking of those names off that polling subdivision was done by Judge Meyers, a gentleman who represented the Liberal -cause in the constituency in which I
have the honour to reside for many years and who was an ardent Liberal politician. He was the judge appointed. He did noting illegal. Why ? Because the district was divided by the redistribution and he had to divide the lists. Under the provincial law it was referred to a judge. Judge Meyers divided it and yet this hon. gentleman states it was done by a Tory and that if it had been done by a Grit he would have been placed in the penitentiary. Surely the hon. member for Portage la Prairie does not want to put Judge Meyers in the penitentiary for carrying out the provisions of the law. There was no more ardent admirer of his than the hon. member for Porta., e la Prairie in days gone by. He was appointed by this government. He did so under the powers given him by Act of parliament coupled with an order in council. The order in council is right here under my hand appointing Judge Meyers. I have a certified copy of that order in council in my possession. The Act which gave the judge authority to strike these names off the list is chapter 23 of the statutes of Manitoba, 1806, section 7 and subsection 4 coupled with an order in council, No. 11465. The changes in the voters' list for the electoral division above mentioned were occasioned by the fact that the boundaries of these electoral divisions were changed by chapter 11 of the statutes of Manitoba, 1907. And by a perusal of subsection 4, section 7, chapter 23, statutes of Manitoba, 1906, it will be seen that provision is made for changes in the revised voters' lists by a judge in the county court of the province to be nominated and appointed by an order in council whenever the territory comprised in an electoral division has been changed ; so that, in making changes in these electorial divisions, Judge Meyers and Judge Ryan, in another district, were each acting within their . jurisdiction and in accordance with the law.
At page 349 of ' Hansard ' it will be seen that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie said, in reply to a question of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Bennett), as to whether these names had been struck off in open court ' no court, they simply did it on the side and it was all right.' I tell you that it was done in open court and that it was done by Judge Meyers acting within his jurisdiction according to chapter 23 of the statutes of Manitoba for 1906, to which I have already referred. Then, again, at page 349 of ' Hansard,' it will be seen that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie made this statement :
They take from one electoral division and add to another, hut they fail to make the necessary provision for the correction of the voters' lists.
This is as unfortunate as the statement that he made previously that these names were ' not struck off in open court but simply on the side and It was all right,' be-
And they are all Liberal judges.

The government need have no fear of the judges because they are all appointees of the Do-

minion government. If the Frime Minister acts on my suggestion which is a fair one, it will do away with the necessity of introducing such a Bill as this which perpetrates a rank injustice on the people of the west.
And the voters could be notified of where they are to vote.

Yes, and at the same time the people could he notified and know at what poll they should vote. The Minister of Justice told us the other day :
We are not only adopting the provincial lists in their entirety as the basis upon which revision and appeal takes place but in addition we follow completely the provincial method of preparing and revising the lists.
But this method has been condemned by the hon. gentlemen opposite and yet the Minister of Justice says they are going to follow completely the provisions of the provincial law and to adopt the provincial lists in their entirety.
And the lists are made in accordance with whatever laws the provinces choose to enact for their own purpose, as was the intention when the statute of 1908 was passed. That is an outline of the first clause of this Bill.
And yet hon. gentlemen opposite get up and denounce the present method of compiling the present lists in Manitoba, and their own minister says he will adopt these lists in their entirety, in order to have a revision. But the whole object and the whole motive behind the Bill is to have the preparation of the lists pass into the hands of partisan officials of this government. That is the whole secret of the Bill and from our experience of the past we know just exactly how much fairness we can expect from those gentlemen in the preparation and revision of the lists.
I shall not discuss the provisions of the Bill as it affects other provinces, but as was justly pointed out so far as it relates to the unorganized districts of Ontario and Quebec it would work out in practice that all the navvies working on the Grand Trunk Pacific, who are under the influence of the contractors who are in turn under the influence of the government, would be placed upon the list and would be polled holus bolus in favour of the Liberal candidates. At any rate that is the object and intention of the Bill. The hon. member of Winnipeg (Mr. Bole) stated that there was an educational test in Manitoba which necessitated the voter being able to read the Manitoba Act in one of several languages, and lie told ns that was designed to disfranchise certain foreigners. But, at the same time he told us there was a clause in the Dominion Act by which they were going to vote the Galicians and, he said : I am going. to poll the Gallician vote. He spoke about them as if he was herding a lot of cattle ; he told us that he was going to poll the Galician vote. Yes, that is the way they did it in my own constituency. They had their homestead inspector, they had their interpreters, they had a Mounted Policeman all the way from Regina standing at the door with his side arms, and we know what influence that had on Galicians who were practically serfs in their native country. We had them standing there threatening them that they would have to serve in the army if they voted Conservative and that they would have their homesteads taken from them. The Galician interpreter was arrested with $600 in $2 bills in his pockets starting out to influence the voters on Sunday morning and he and the $600 were tied up during election week. The member for Winnipeg told us that he was going to poll the Galicians, they are not going to have much to say in it themselves, but he is going to vote them just like so many cattle. Now, this provision for voting the employees on the Transcontinental railroad is quite apparent, and although it is only a blind to put it in this Bill I am glad in one way it is associated with this outrage on the province of Manitoba. We have had an overture made to drop the unorganized territories in Ontario and Quebec and to drop British Columbia from the Bill, but the object is to get at Manitoba. They simply associate the other provinces with us in the Bill so as not to make it appear so transparent, but the overture made shows exactly the animus by which they are influenced.
I throw out a warning to the Prime Minister. I tell him that he has no idea of the feeling that has been raised in the west by the introduction of this Bill. I was surprised on a recent visit to my province to find no Liberals justifying the Bill, while every Conservative condemned it. The fair minded Liberals will not stand for it, and I tell the Prime Minister he is being misled, if he believes what his supporters have told him that there is any outcry in Manitoba against the method of preparing the prorfn-cial lists under the present provincial law, he will find many honest Liberals in that province to tell him otherwise. Why was it that the Liberal candidates throughout the last provincial campaign had scarcely a word said as to the method of preparing the voters' lists ? I never heard the thing discussed in the four constituencies I had the privilege of speaking in. The Prime Minister has no idea of the bitter feeling that has been engendered in Manitoba by this Bill, and it will not redound to his reputation for fairness as a statesman to force upon an unwilling province an Act of this most objectionable character. At the worst it will invite retaliation. I am not going to say that the provincial government will retaliate, but I do know that when the provincial government came into power and

when Hugh John Macdonald wiped out that Greenway Election Act which was described by Mr. James Fisher, an independent Liberal, as a monstrosity of monstrosities, there were a great many in the province of Manitoba who thought it was a mistake to repeal the Greenway law for they claimed it should be retained so as to give the Liberals a dose of their own medicine and let them know what it was to run an election under such an Act. If this Bill is forced upon an unwilling opposition in this House there may be a temptation to retaliate, and if so the last state of the Liberals in that province will be worse than the first, for to-day they are disunited, disintegrated, unable, to secure a seat for their outside leader, and with their inside leader endorsing the voters' lists as at present prepared in the province of Manitoba.
Without any investigation this Act has been introduced. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has made a challenge. I wmuld like to see that challenge accepted. If they are going to force on Manitoba the making of voters' lists by Dominion officials, why should that not be done in other provinces if it can be established that other provinces have voters' lists and Franchise Acts far more unfair to political opponents than those in Manitoba? We have never had any investigation into this question, and the leader of the opposition has stated that if an opportunity is afforded he will bring forward two voters disfranchised in Nova Scotia by means of the operation of the Franchise Act there to one in Manitoba. This being the case, why should we be forced to accept such a Bill as this without any investigation? It is unjust and unfair and as a Manitoban I protest. I go still further. I do not wish to use words that may be interpreted as a threat, I do not desire them to be interpreted in that way, but I say, as has been said by other hon. members, that the opposition would be justified in refusing a dollar of supplies to carry on this government until that obnoxious measure is withdrawn. The First Minister knows the constitutional privileges which an opposition hi ay utilize to fight for what they consider their rights. He has occupied that position in days gone by. He objected to the Franchise Act of 1885 with all the resources on which he could call, and I say It Is impossible for an opposition here to calmly submit. There is a limit to the forbearance and we would be justified in refusing supplies until that Bill is modified to the extent of having the obnoxious provision relating to Manitoba and British Columbia withdrawn. There has been no complaint by any members from British Columbia as to the voters' lists there. The clauses which relate to the unorganized districts of Ontario and Quebec fall within the same category. I, therefore, feel in duty bound to move the following amendment :

That all the words after the word ' that ' in the proposed motion be omitted, and the following substituted instead thereof:
This House affirms that the Dominion Elections Act should be effectively amended during the present session in order to prevent corrupt practices and ensure honest elections, but that the discrimination against the provinces of Manitoba and British Columbia created by the first section of the proposed Bill is not founded upon any inquiry, evidence, report or sufficient information, is a radical departure from the principle of acceptance of provincial voters' lists and is invidious and unjustifiable.

Mr. Speaker, the closing remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat are almost sufficient, without any other reason, to make every honest Liberal and possibly every honest citizen of this country seriously consider the situation. The closing remarks of the hon. gentleman's speech were practically a hold-up for this House and a challenge for the Liberals of this country. In fact, his entire speech was along the line of trying to prove that the Conservatives were more honest tbaii the Liberals; that idea underlay his whole argument. I shall not follow his remarks in detail, but I would say to the Prime Minister that he need not be the least alarmed as to the feeling in Manitoba towards this legislation. I can assure the Prime Minister that this legislation has the warmest kind of support from the majority of the people of Manitoba.
I shall refer to some of the opening remarks of my bon. friend and leave it to the House to judge whether we may accept any part of them as being in keeping with the facts. He referred to certain work that was being done in connection with registration in Manitoba at the present time; be tried to make out that fair and liberal treatment was meted out to the people there with the exception of one or two cases. But in reading the order in council in regard to the situation and the time given for work in connection with the revision of the list, he did not keep in touch with the facts. In speaking of Beautiful Plains he tried to read from this order in council that there were four clear days between the closing of the registration and the revision, while there were only three. In the Gladstone division he claimed there were twelve clear days, while there were only eight. If the rest of his statements are no nearer the truth than that, the House will not put very much credence in what he says.
- Mr. STAPLES. Will you be satisfied that your grievance is remedied if the time is extended in the particular places you have in mind ?

I shall be better satisfied than I am to-day but not completely satisfied, because I am convinced that if

this agitation were not on here to-day, if this legislation were not before the House, I would not be getting a promise of that kind.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me ? Who fixes the dates for the courts of revision ?	.

The Lieutenant Governor in Council-the political machine of the province of Manitoba. It is not the judges, as our Tory friends throughout the country would lead the people to believe. The judges have no control over the courts of revision as to fixing dates.
The hon. member for Marquette said it was the judges.
There were only eight clear days in Gladstone and three in Beautiful Plains.
The last date for the court of registration in Gladstone is May 28, and the court of revision 9th June. Can you make eight days out of that ?
I will read it and show the hon. gentleman he is not correct.
I am quoting from the ' Gazette.'
June 1, for the court of revision in the electoral division of Gladstone ; in the town hall of Gladstone on June 9. In all eight clear days. The hon. gentleman said to-night there were twelve days.

In justice to myself let me point out that the latest court of registration is usually that at the foot of the list. The last notice of the registration clerk at the foot of the list is usually the last court of revision, and in this case it was set at the 28th May. But I notice that above there was a court of revision advertised for June 1, which I overlooked. I took the notice at the foot of the list as being the last court.
You will have to revise the rest of your speech.

In connection with the proposed legislation I do not think there is any better evidence this House can have for the securing of something along this line than the fact that throughout the country, for the last four years, mere have been hurled at the Liberal party statements of the most extravagant kind imaginable as to what they did in the elections of 1904. The discussion here up to the present has gone to prove that we have an undesirable condition of affairs in connection with the conduct of the elections in Manitoba and that there is need for some remedy. I have spoken on this question every session since the election of 1904 and have taken the 256
position that the conditions surrounding the running of elections in the province of Manitoba are such that we ought not to tolerate. A great part of the long speech we have just heard was spent on a comparison between the Greenway legislation and that of the Roblin government, trying to prove that the latter was better than the former. But so far as we on this side are concerned, that is not an issue because in this Bill we adopt the legislation of Manitoba. And while I do not approve of the Manitoba law in its entirety and propose to show where I take exception to it, the greatest trouble we have in that province lies in the administration of the law. The provincial government have taken full conu-ol of the administration of the law. No official or judge has anything to say as to how that law shall be administered. The full control is taken by the executive council.
Do not the judges revise the lists ?

Only on the direction of the executive council and only during the hours fixed by the executive council. Let me give you an idea how that works out. In the Beautiful Plains division where I live, the necessary time is not provided to make a proper revision of the list. The time allowed by the executive council of Manitoba to revise the list is five hours in a day from 1 to 6 o'clock p.m. Only during those hours can the judge act in connection with the revision of the lists. Is that fair ? The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) complained bitterly of the conditions under the Greenway Act and he referred to Beautiful Plains, where he said the list was stuffed to the extent of 107 names. But what was the condition last year ? There wei'e almost 600 names to be adjusted in connection with that list in that same division last year. We succeeded in striking off 319 names and adding 184. How does that compare as against a list stuffed with 107 names ? And how did we get this adjustment ? Was it by law ? Not at all. We had to meet our Tory opposition independent of the courts, and only at the will of our opposition friends did we succeed in getting any of those names off. If we had gone into the courts and argued, we would not have got 10 off. And after getting those few adjusted in that amicable way, there were 75 or 100 more that should have gone off but on which we could not agree. That is the kind of administration we are getting in Manitoba. The condition is not endurable and does not compare in any way with the conditions under the Greenway legislation of some years ago which is so condemned by our Tory friends.
In connection with this whole matter, I am satisfied that the people are tired of the situation. I am satisfied that the people, particularly in the province of Manitoba,



are tired of hearing about those 9,000 names which were disfranchised by the red line. They are tired of hearing about what was done, or supposed to be done, in the way of irregularities in 1904. I know that the Liberals of Manitoba are convinced that the law for running Dominion elections is bad and they want to have better arrangements. I am satisfied that our Tory friends came to the conclusion that the situation is not right, as proven by the fact that, for three or four years, they have had charges standing against Dominion officials and they have spent thousands and thousands of dollars of our money trying to secure convictions and finally quit the job without succeeding. They must have come to the conclusion that the situation is bad and that there should be some remedy for it. I think that is the conviction of the honest-minded people of this country generally. Now, if the law is in such a shape that wrongs of that kind can be committed, 1 think it is up to this government to provide such legislation as will prevent such wrongs in the future. On the other hand, there should be some law that would provide for the protection of these officers. If these acts were legal acts, acts that it was proper for these officials to do, I think this country should give them protection ; something should be done for these people who have been persecuted and hounded for the last four or five years. I take the position that no wrongs were done, but that, in adjusting the lists, of 1904 as they did, the returning officers did what they had a right to do. And what I take exception to here as mentioned by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) that when some of our Tory friends did the same things of which complaint is made against Liberals, they were not prosecuted by the authorities of the province ; they were allowed to go scot free while the Liberals were hounded. I think we want to get something that will get us away from this whole trouble and agitation.

Before the hon. gentleman leaves that point, will he allow me to ask him a question ? He belongs to Manitoba, and I want to understand the situation as a citizen of the Dominion. I think he said there was a hardship in these judges not having time to revise the lists. Will he tell me of any case in which a judge refused to adjourn a court to another day when he was not through with this work ?
I can tell him that Mr. Heap
I do not want to know about him.

He was sitting as a judge and had the powers of a judge so
far as his work was concerned-
I do not care about Leach. There are judges in Manitoba, and the hon. gentleman knows what a judge is. And these judges are reputable men.
I am speaking of Mr. Heap.

I would like the hon. gentleman, if he will, to answer my question. I am talking about the judges of the province of Manitoba. He said that there is not time for them to do their work. I ask him, can he give an occasion where any of these judges who did the revising refused to adjourn a court when he was not through with the work of revising ? If he cannot tell me that, I would like him to say so.

The order in council is imperative, and where a judge adjourns his court for the purpose of placing men on the list who were not on, the attorney general of the province took the position that it was an illegal act and he took those names off the list-at least approved of the taking the names off.

Will the hon. gentleman kindly tell me what was the name of the judge when it did happen ?
Mi\ CRAWFORD. Mr. Heap was the revising officer. Now, in connection with the working out of the situation in Manitoba in the last election, I take the position that the returning officers did their work and did it as they had a right to do. But, at the same time, I must say that they were put in a position which they should not be asked to occupy. Section 24 of the Dominion Elections Act provides :
The polling divisions shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be those established by or under the laws of the province for the purpose of provincial elections within the territory comprised in the electoral district for which the election is held.
Now, in the situation as it existed in 1904, in Manitoba, there were no polling divisions established by law.
The judge in the court of appeals said there were.
I challenge any hon. gentlemen opposite to show and define any polling division established in the province of Manitoba by law.
I would accept the challenge and say I defeat the hon. gentleman by quoting the fact that the court of appeal of the province of Manitoba said that there were-and that is pretty good authority.
Chief Justice Howell, of the court of appeal of Manitoba, before the special committee two years ago, made the statement made by the hon. member of Portage la Prairie (Mr. Crawford).
And lie was overruled by bis colleagues.
His judgment was appealed from and overruled, and he-
He was not overruled at all.
He was overruled by the full coui't, and my hon. and learned friend (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) ought to know that.

I make that statement and I have yet to find out that any poll was so established. I have read the evidence taken before the committee, and even If you take the statement made by the hon. member for Marquette, you will see that they do not say there was a poll established.
Certainly they do.
No, they say that If it did exist the officer had a right to do so and so.
They said it did not exist.
That was before the revision.

That was before the revision. In connection with that law the people had ample time to examine the lists to see whether their names were on, or what names were left off and then there was a reasonable time allowed to appeal, a sufficient time granted to give the people every opportunity to have a complete and fair list. But, what are the conditions of this legislation that hon. gentlemen say is all right and should not be interfered with at the present time ? There is no time fixed by statute as to how long a time shall intervene between the registration and the sitting of the court of revision. This whole power is vested in the executive council and they can manipulate it according to their own sweet will. Here to-day in my own district, at my own home, where I live, in Beautiful Plains, the full time allowed for compiling and revising the whole list, where there are hundreds of names changed, is only sixteen days. In Gladstone, which is 100 miles long, the time allowed is only seventeen days. There is no comparison at all as to how the system is worked out under the Acts of Greenway and Roblin and his associates. IVe have in this proposed legislation practically decided to accept the situation so far as the law of the province is concerned and we can give sufficient and reasonable time for that work. I would say, however, that it would please me much if we could adopt the Act of 1902 of the Roblin government which places in the hands of the judges complete control of making the voters' lists, including the appointment of registration clerks. That is the kind of legislation I. would like to see so far as the preparation of the voters' lists is concerned
That is not the legislation before the House.
No.
Are you voting for or against the legislation before the House?

The legislation of 1902, to which I have referred, would please me much better than any other proposed. We have got to have something of this kind and the present Bill will meet the requirements if we cannot get anything better.
I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
